summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would establish a security framework for federal courts and specified tribunals, with powers for appointed officers, court security offences and safeguards.
It would give officers powers to request screening and searches, control entry and remove people, with detention available only in specified circumstances.
The framework would extend to the Administrative Appeals Tribunal and the Family Court of Western Australia, as well as federal courts and other prescribed tribunals.
changes: Security officers could detain suspected offenders to prevent violence or serious property damage and deliver them promptly to police.
Unauthorised recording or transmission of proceedings and related events would become an offence, subject to exceptions.
Courts exercising family law jurisdiction could make protective orders, which would have to allow access for legitimate court business.
Appointed officers would face qualification and identification requirements, with complaints and oversight arrangements for their conduct.
summary.affected: Court users, court staff, judicial officers, security officers and authorised court officers are affected.

speeches.speaker: Mark Dreyfus
speeches.brief: Introduced the companion Court Security (Consequential Amendments) Bill, which removes overlapping provisions from the 1971 Public Order Act to allow the new Court Security Bill's framework to operate cleanly across federal courts and tribunals.

speeches.speaker: Michael Keenan
speeches.brief: Explained the Court Security Bill will replace the outdated Public Order Act with a modern framework giving trained security officers powers to search, screen and detain people at risk at Commonwealth courts including the Family Court of Western Australia and the Administrative Appeals Tribunal, with oversight from the Commonwealth Ombudsman.

speeches.speaker: Michael McCormack
speeches.brief: Backed the Court Security Bill as a necessary update to the outdated 1971 Public Order Act, noting family courts in particular are places where emotion can boil over into fear, intimidation and violence, and said uniform new security arrangements will apply across all Commonwealth courts and tribunals.

speeches.speaker: Shayne Neumann
speeches.brief: Summed up the Court Security Bill, drawing on more than two decades practising family law to describe the stress, anger and hostility courts can see, and said the new powers for security and authorised court officers come with licensing, training and identification safeguards plus continued reliance on police for the most serious incidents.

speeches.speaker: Penny Wong
speeches.brief: The Court Security Bill 2013 and companion bill replace the outdated 1971 Public Order Act, granting federal courts and tribunals new powers for security officers—including screening, search, and limited use of force—with safeguards such as licensing, training, and Commonwealth Ombudsman oversight.

speeches.speaker: Gary Humphries
speeches.brief: The coalition supported the Court Security Bill 2013 and associated bill, which expand security powers for Commonwealth courts and tribunals, including the Family Court of Western Australia and the Administrative Appeals Tribunal, to address modern security concerns raised by federal court heads.
